entry: Sport of riding a wave toward the shore on a board. Ancient cultures often surfed on their bellies and knees, and the [[Moche culture|Moche]] of [[Peru]] used reed craft. Modern surfing is most often stand-up surfing, which has three major subdivisions: stand-up paddling, longboarding and shortboarding. In tow-in surfing, a motorized watercraft pulls the surfer into a large wave. The North Shore of Oahu, in [[Hawaii]], is known for some of the world's best winter waves. As of 2023, the Guinness Book of World Records recognized a 26.2 m (86 ft) wave ride by Sebastian Steudtner at Nazaré, Portugal, as the largest wave ever surfed. Surfing was added to the Olympic program by the International Olympic Committee in 2016, with competition debuting at the 2020 Summer Olympics in Japan.

Country on the northern coast of [[South America]] (pop., 2021: 612,985), considered part of the [[Caribbean]] region. Over 95% of its territory is covered by [[Rainforest|rainforest]]. It is the smallest sovereign country in South America by population and territory, and Paramaribo, the capital, has roughly half the population. Indigenous peoples inhabited the area as early as the fourth millennium BC, and the Dutch controlled much of it by the late 17th century. Under Dutch rule it was a plantation colony focused on sugar, and approximately 300,000 enslaved Africans were taken there in the [[Atlantic slave trade|transatlantic slave trade]]. After slavery was abolished in 1863, indentured workers came from British India and the [[Dutch East Indies]]. Suriname became independent on November 25, 1975. Dutch is the official language, and Sranan Tongo, an English-based creole, is a [[Lingua franca|lingua franca]]. The economy depends on [[Bauxite|bauxite]], gold, petroleum and agricultural products.

Mostly hereditary portion of a [[Personal name|personal name]] that indicates one's family. It is typically combined with a given name to form a full name. A surname may also be called a last name, particularly in [[American English]], but some cultures place it at the start of a name. Most people have one surname, but in Portuguese-speaking and many Spanish-speaking countries, two are used for legal purposes, one from each parent. English surnames, documented in the 11th century, began with reference to a trade, a father's name, a birthplace or physical features, and were not necessarily inherited. By 1400 most English families, and those from Lowland Scotland, had adopted hereditary surnames. In China, according to legend, family names began with Emperor Fu Xi in 2000 BC. The study of proper names is called onomastics.

Rapid, fleeting mental and physiological state produced by an unexpected event. It is related to the startle response, which interrupts an ongoing action and reorients attention to a new, possibly significant event. Surprise can be pleasant, unpleasant or neutral, and its intensity ranges from slight to strong enough to induce the fight-or-flight response. Carroll Izard and Paul Ekman include surprise among the primary or basic emotions, and consider it evolutionarily adaptive, innate and universal across human cultures. Surprise represents the difference between expectations and reality, and in interpersonal communication, the Expectancy Violation Theory links it to violations of expectations shaped by [[Social norm|social norms]] and other factors. Surprises can make people aware of their own ignorance, which can open a window to new knowledge.

Art and cultural movement that developed in Europe in the aftermath of [[World War I]]. Surrealists sought to let the unconscious mind express itself, often through illogical or dreamlike scenes. Its leader, André Breton, intended to resolve dream and reality into a "super-reality," and he regarded the movement above all as a revolutionary one associated with [[Communism]] and [[Anarchism]]. Surrealism was influenced by [[Dada]]. The term was coined by Guillaume Apollinaire in 1917, but the movement was not officially established until after October 1924, when Breton's Surrealist Manifesto claimed the name. The most important center was [[Paris]], and from the 1920s the movement spread around the globe, producing painting, writing, photography, theater, film and music.

Formal capitulation of the [[Empire of Japan]] to the Allies, ending [[World War II]]. Emperor [[Hirohito]] announced the surrender on August 15, 1945; it was formally signed on September 2 aboard USS Missouri. The United States dropped atomic bombs on [[Hiroshima]] on August 6 and [[Nagasaki]] on August 9, and the [[Soviet Union]] declared war on Japan on August 8. The role of the atomic bombings in the surrender remains debated. The state of war formally ended when the Treaty of San Francisco came into force on April 28, 1952.

Ceremonial county in South East England, bordered by [[Greater London]] to the northeast, [[Kent]] to the east, and [[Hampshire]] and [[Berkshire]] to the west. The county covers 1,663 sq km (642 square miles) and had an estimated population of 1,248,649 in 2024. Its largest settlement is Woking. Its north forms part of the Greater London conurbation. The North Downs, a chalk escarpment, divides the densely populated north from the more rural south. Surrey has the densest woodland cover in England, at 22.4 percent. It is one of the home counties.

Arrangement in which a woman carries and gives birth to a child for another person or couple who will become the child's legal parents. People pursue it for reasons including [[Infertility|infertility]], dangers of [[Pregnancy|pregnancy]], or when pregnancy is a medical impossibility. The person giving birth is the gestational carrier, and the intended parents take custody after birth. Monetary compensation may or may not be involved. Legality and cost vary widely between jurisdictions, contributing to fertility tourism. Surrogacy was first achieved in April 1986, when an [[Embryo|embryo]] created by in vitro fertilization was transferred to a gestational carrier.

Systematic observation and monitoring of a person, population or location, for information-gathering, influencing, managing or directing. It is widely used by [[Government|governments]] for law enforcement and [[National security|national security]], and by criminal organizations and businesses. Methods include human interaction, postal interception, closed-circuit television (CCTV) cameras, wiretapping and data mining. Automated systems sift intercepted [[Internet]] traffic for trigger words or contact with suspicious individuals. [[Civil liberties|Civil liberties]] activists often criticize it as an unjustified violation of [[Privacy|privacy]]. Democracies may have laws restricting surveillance, whereas authoritarian governments seldom have domestic restrictions. Improvements in technology have led to mass and global surveillance, and government and intelligence agencies have obtained consumer data through online purchases. [[Espionage|Espionage]] is covert and typically illegal under the observed party's rules.

Field of applied [[Statistics|statistics]] that studies survey methods, concentrating on human-research surveys. It covers the [[Sampling (statistics)|sampling]] of individual units from a population and techniques of data collection, such as questionnaire construction and methods for improving the number and accuracy of responses. Survey methodologists must decide how to identify sample members, contact hard-to-reach respondents, test questions, choose the mode of data collection and adjust estimates for identified errors. Polls and public-health surveys exemplify quantitative research that uses survey methodology. Although [[Census|censuses]] include no sample, they use questionnaires, interviewers and non-response follow-up. Surveys inform marketing research, [[Psychology|psychology]], transportation studies, health-care provision and [[Sociology|sociology]].

Technique, profession, art and science of determining the terrestrial positions of points from the [[Distance|distances]] and [[Angle|angles]] between them. Surveyors draw on geodesy, geometry, trigonometry, regression analysis and physics, using equipment such as total stations, [[Theodolite|theodolites]], GNSS receivers, drones and [[Lidar|lidar]] sensors. Surveying has been part of human development since recorded history began, and it is used in most forms of construction, transportation, mapping and the definition of legal land boundaries. In [[Ancient Egypt|ancient Egypt]], a rope stretcher re-established boundaries after the annual floods of the Nile. The almost perfect squareness of the [[Great Pyramid of Giza]], built c. 2700 BC, reflects Egyptian command of surveying. In 1086, [[William the Conqueror]] commissioned the [[Domesday Book]], which recorded landowners and land quality but did not include maps showing exact locations.

Ruler of the [[Khmer Empire]] (r. 1113–1150). He is best known as the builder of [[Angkor Wat]], the largest Hindu temple in the world, which he dedicated to Vishnu and [[Shiva]]. Reaching the throne through a contest with rival claimants, he reunited the empire, and vassals paid him tribute. His monumental architecture, military campaigns and restoration of strong government have led historians to rank him among the empire's greatest rulers. He sent a mission to the [[Chola dynasty]] of south India and presented a precious stone to Chola Emperor Kulothunga Chola I in 1114. His eastern campaigns against [[Champa]] were largely unsuccessful, although in 1145 he appears to have invaded it and sacked its capital, Vijaya. The first syllables of his name are a [[Sanskrit]] root meaning *sun*.

Ancient city in the lower [[Zagros Mountains]] of Iran, about 250 km (160 mi) east of the [[Tigris]]. It served as the capital of [[Elam]] and the winter capital of the [[Achaemenid Empire]], and remained a strategic center during the Parthian and Sasanian periods. Its name is of Elamite origin. The city appears in early [[Sumer|Sumerian]] records and in the [[Hebrew Bible]] as Shushan, chiefly in the Book of Esther, where Esther becomes queen. The [[Aeschylus]] play *The Persians* is set there. Excavations after 1885 were organized by the French government; Jacques de Morgan excavated from 1897 until 1911, and many artifacts were taken to the [[Louvre]].

American social reformer and [[Women's rights|women's rights]] activist who played a pivotal role in the [[Women's suffrage|women's suffrage]] movement. Born into a Quaker family, she collected anti-slavery petitions at the age of 17 and in 1856 became New York state agent for the American Anti-Slavery Society. In 1851 she met [[Elizabeth Cady Stanton]], her lifelong friend and co-worker. During the Civil War they founded the Women's Loyal National League, which collected nearly 400,000 signatures for the abolition of slavery. They began publishing *The Revolution*, a women's rights newspaper, in 1868, and a year later founded the National Woman Suffrage Association. In 1872 Anthony was arrested in [[Rochester, New York]] for voting and was convicted in a widely publicized trial. In 1878 she and Stanton arranged for an amendment giving women the vote to be presented to Congress; it became the Nineteenth Amendment in 1920.

American actor and social activist. She was born in Jackson Heights, [[Queens]]. She won the Academy Award for Best Actress for playing Helen Prejean in *Dead Man Walking* (1995). She gained prominence in the musical horror film *The Rocky Horror Picture Show* (1975). Her other films include *Bull Durham* (1988), *Little Women* (1994) and *The Lovely Bones* (2009). Her awards include a British Academy Film Award and nominations for seven Emmy Awards and ten Golden Globes. Sarandon was appointed a [[UNICEF]] Goodwill Ambassador in 1999. She played [[Bette Davis]] in the FX miniseries *Feud* (2017).

Traditional Japanese dish of vinegared [[Rice|rice]] combined with seafood, vegetables or meat. Hanaya Yohei is believed to have created the modern form around 1824 in the [[Edo period]], inventing nigiri-zushi, in which seafood is placed on hand-pressed vinegared rice. An early form, narezushi, preserved fish by fermenting it in rice; the method may have originated in [[Southeast Asia]], possibly in the [[Mekong|Mekong]] River basin. Lacto-fermentation prevented the fish from spoiling, and after wet-field rice cultivation was introduced in the Yayoi period, narezushi became an important source of protein for Japanese consumers. Sushi is commonly prepared with squid, eel, yellowtail, salmon, [[Tuna|tuna]] or imitation crab, and it is often served with pickled ginger, [[Wasabi|wasabi]] and [[Soy sauce|soy sauce]]. It is considered one of the most popular dishes in the world.

Heterogeneous [[Mixture|mixture]] of a fluid containing solid particles large enough to settle out over time. Particles usually must be larger than one micrometer, and they eventually settle; sand in water is a typical example. Its particles are visible under a [[Microscope|microscope]] and settle if left undisturbed. A suspension differs from a [[Colloid|colloid]], whose particles are smaller and do not settle, and from a [[Solution (chemistry)|solution]], in which the solute does not exist as a solid. A suspension of liquid droplets or fine solid particles in a gas is an [[Aerosol|aerosol]]. In the atmosphere, suspended particulates include fine dust, [[Soot|soot]], sea salt, biogenic and [[Volcano|volcano]] sulfates, [[Nitrate|nitrate]], and cloud droplets. Suspensions are thermodynamically unstable but can be kinetically stable for a long time, which can determine a suspension's shelf life. Multiple light scattering is the most widely used technique to monitor a product's dispersion state.

1977 Italian supernatural [[Horror film|horror film]] directed by Dario Argento, who co-wrote it with Daria Nicolodi. It is partly based on Thomas De Quincey's 1845 essay *Suspiria de Profundis*. An American ballet student arrives in Freiburg, [[West Germany]], to study at a prestigious dance academy and realizes after a series of murders that the school is a front for something sinister. It is the first film of Argento's Three Mothers trilogy. Its score by Argento and the progressive rock band Goblin has been praised, and it inspired a 2018 film of the same title, directed by Luca Guadagnino.

Ability to continue over a long period of time; in modern usage, a state in which the environment, [[Economy|economy]] and [[Society|society]] continue to exist. Many definitions emphasize the environmental dimension, including problems such as [[Climate change|climate change]] and biodiversity loss. A related concept is [[Sustainable development|sustainable development]]; UNESCO describes sustainability as a long-term goal and sustainable development as the processes and pathways to achieve it. Scholars debate the economic dimension under the concepts of weak and strong sustainability, and separating [[Economic growth|economic growth]] from environmental harm such as [[Pollution|pollution]] is difficult. Sustainability is hard to measure because the concept is complex, contextual and dynamic, and no fixed definition of its indicators exists. Critics argue that the concept is vague, a buzzword, or even an impossible goal.

Form of [[Agriculture|farming]] that reduces environmental harm and expands natural resources, and ensures that non-renewable resources are harnessed for productive purposes. Methods include permaculture, agroforestry, mixed farming, multiple cropping and crop rotation, and they aim to prevent adverse effects on [[Soil|soil]], water and [[Biodiversity|biodiversity]]. Agriculture has a large environmental footprint, playing a role in [[Climate change|climate change]]: food systems are responsible for one third of anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions, and farming also contributes to water scarcity, water pollution, land degradation and [[Deforestation|deforestation]]. A common consensus holds that sustainable farming is the most realistic way to feed growing populations. Meta-analyses of field trials report that sustainable or organic variants average 19-25% lower output than conventional systems, and critics question whether broad adoption could feed projected populations without expanding cultivated land.

Approach to growth and human development that aims to meet the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. It seeks a society where living conditions and resources meet human needs without undermining planetary integrity, balancing the economy, environment and [[Society|society]]. The 1987 Brundtland Report, *Our Common Future*, helped make the concept better known. The Rio Process, begun at the 1992 Earth Summit in [[Rio de Janeiro]], placed the concept on the international agenda. It is the foundational concept of the Sustainable Development Goals for 2030, adopted in 2015 by the [[United Nations]] General Assembly, which address [[Poverty|poverty]], [[Climate change|climate change]], [[Biodiversity|biodiversity]] loss and [[Peace|peace]]. Scholars have described the concept as open-ended, ambiguous and incoherent, and some call it an oxymoron, since development is inherently unsustainable.

Prefecture-level city in [[Jiangsu]] province, eastern [[China]], and a major industrial hub specializing in high-end manufacturing. Known as the cradle of Wu culture, it was founded in 514 BC and grew into a city along the [[Grand Canal (China)|Grand Canal]]. From the 10th century onward it was an important economic and cultural center, and it was the largest non-capital city in the world until it was overtaken by [[Shanghai]] in about 1850. Its gardens, [[Silk|silk]] production and Kunqu [[Opera|opera]] are long admired; the classical gardens were added to the UNESCO list of [[World Heritage Site|World Heritage Sites]] in 1997 and 2000. Since [[Reform and opening up|reform and opening up]] began in 1978, Suzhou has attained GDP growth rates of about 14% in 35 years, and it had 5 million registered residents in 2023.

Norwegian [[Archipelago|archipelago]] in the Arctic Ocean, lying about midway between northern Norway and the [[North Pole]]. Its largest island is Spitsbergen, and its largest settlement is [[Longyearbyen]]. Whalers used the islands as a base in the 17th and 18th centuries, and coal mining began at the start of the 20th century. The Svalbard Treaty of 1920 recognizes Norwegian sovereignty, makes the archipelago a free economic zone and restricts its military use. Approximately 60% of the archipelago is covered by [[Glacier|glaciers]]. Its Arctic climate is significantly warmer than other areas at the same latitude, owing to the tail end of the [[Gulf Stream]]. Seven national parks and twenty-three nature reserves cover two-thirds of the archipelago, which is home to [[Polar bear|polar bears]], reindeer and seabirds. Norway announced new [[Tourism|tourism]] regulations in February 2024, including a maximum of 200 people on a ship.

Swedish physicist and chemist, one of the founders of [[Physical chemistry|physical chemistry]]. His 1884 dissertation on electrolytic conductivity proposed that solid salts dissociate into charged [[Ion|ions]] when dissolved, even without an electric current. Extensions of this work earned him the [[Nobel Prize]] in Chemistry in 1903, making him the first Swedish laureate. In 1905 he became director of the Nobel Institute, where he remained until his death. He was the first to use the principles of physical chemistry to estimate how far increases in atmospheric [[Carbon dioxide|carbon dioxide]] are responsible for rising surface temperature, work that played an important role in the emergence of modern climate science. The [[Arrhenius equation]] and Arrhenius acid and base are named after him.

Ruler of [[Great Moravia]] (r. 870–894). Under him the realm reached its maximum territorial extent, encompassing parts of modern [[Czech Republic]], Slovakia, Poland and Hungary. In 870 he deposed his uncle Rastislav and betrayed him to the [[Franks]]. After the Moravians rebelled against the Franks, he was released and led the rebels to victory. Later he paid tribute to East Francia under the 874 peace treaty concluded at Forchheim, but expanded his territories elsewhere. The [[Holy See]] took his people under its protection in 880, and [[Pope]] Stephen V addressed him as "King" in a letter of 885. In 886 he expelled the disciples of [[Cyril and Methodius|Methodius]] from Moravia, after their teacher's death. After his death the realm collapsed amid a power struggle between his sons and intensifying Hungarian raids.
